 Monday's key developments
 • Campaigning in Kansas : President Donald Trump said riots and looting in France are foreshadowing what could happen to the US if Democrats win in November. And he rejected concerns about the prospects for GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in the surprisingly competitive Senate race in the solid-red state. “The polls are fake,” he said.
 • All eyes on Texas : Early in-person voting began in the Lone Star State, where Democrats are hoping to break through for the first time in 32 years. Voters near Dallas told CNN they are still trying to wrap their minds around the notion that Texas might truly be a battleground state this election. Follow CNN’s early voting tracker here .
 • Voter roll sweep: Federal authorities charged over two dozen foreign nationals in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people who officials say have illegally registered and voted in US elections.

 By Pamela Avila 
 People wait in line to vote early in-person for the midterm elections at the Marty Robbins Recreation Center in El Paso, Texas, on Monday.

 Early in-person voting began today in the Lone Star State, where Democrats were hoping to break through for the first time in 32 years.
 President Donald Trump also rallied in Kansas for GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, and he’ll campaign all week for candidates in North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida and Georgia. And Trump will return to Texas next week.

 Early in-person voting also began today in Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida and South Carolina. North Carolina and Georgia began voting early last week.
 In Kansas tonight , Trump said that riots and looting in France are foreshadowing what could happen to the US if Democrats win in November.
 In the reliably red state, Kansas voters are feeling the economic pinch, with one woman telling CNN the cost of living is the biggest issue motivating her decision on who to vote for. This midterm cycle, Kansas has emerged as one of the most unexpected battlegrounds as Democrats try to pull off their first Senate victory in the state since 1932.

 Trump campaigns in Kansas and offers dark vision if Democrats take control of Congress
 By Kit Maher and Betsy Klein 
 President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas on Monday. 
 Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump offered a dark vision of a Democratic-led Congress in Kansas on Monday night — warning voters of a choice between “radical” Democrats who he said will destroy America or a continuation of what he often calls the “golden age.”
 “Americans are going to stand up and declare that we will defend our culture; we will protect our civilization; we will preserve our religion, our values, and our heritage; and we will never let our nation be conquered or destroyed by people that hate us,” Trump said at a rally in Park City, Kansas.
 “A vote for any Dumo-crat this year is a vote to let that small and dangerous group of extremists hold all of us hostage in America. They’re not going to hold us hostage,” Trump later said.
 He also used the riots in France as a fear-mongering tool, claiming Democrats will “burn it all down” if they take power.
 “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Democrats want to do to America,” Trump said, arguing Democrats would strip away the progress he believes he’s made in his second term.
 “We achieved more in two years than any other presidency in the history of our country. But now the radical left Democrats want to burn it all down. They want to take it all down. Think about France. Think about what we’re witnessing,” Trump said.
 Trump again asked voters to pretend he is on the ballot in an attempt to boost turnout, projecting Republican wins in the House and Senate.
 “The golden age of America is upon us. But you must get out. You must vote Republican. We cannot let these people take it away,” he said.
 Campaigning alongside Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, Trump said Marshall “is all that stands between the people of Kansas and communists controlling the United States Senate.”
 As for Marshall’s opponent in the Senate race, Adam Hamilton, a Democratic pastor, Trump said: “He doesn’t have our views, he doesn’t have our values. … He doesn’t act like a pastor.”

 Trump uses term "Shylock" while defending Sen. Marshall’s lawsuits against his patients
 By Kit Maher 
 President Donald Trump defended Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall against criticism for suing more than 700 patients for outstanding medical bills during his time as an obstetrician-gynecologist, as first reported by The New York Times .
 While defending Marshall, Trump used the term, Shylock, which he’s faced criticism for using in the past and previously claimed ignorance that it’s viewed by some as antisemitic.
 “You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people, and they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” Trump said at a rally in Kansas. “If he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law. He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability.
 In July 2025 , Trump used the same term during a rally in Iowa. He later said he didn’t know the word was viewed by some as antisemitic.
 “I’ve never heard it that way. To me, Shylock is somebody that’s a money lender at high rates,” Trump told reporters at the time. “I’ve never heard it that way, you view it differently than me. I’ve never heard that.”
 The Anti-Defamation League last year condemned the use of the word by Trump, calling it “very troubling and irresponsible.”
 “It underscores how lies and conspiracies about Jews remain deeply entrenched in our country. Words from our leaders matter and we expect more from the President of the United States,” the ADL wrote in a post at the time.
 In 2014 , former President Joe Biden apologized for using the word.

 Trump expresses sympathy after incident at Wichita's Stryker Sports Complex

 President Donald Trump shared his condolences with the Wichita community after an incident this weekend at the Stryker Sports Complex, where a pickup truck sped onto a field where children were playing soccer.
 Two people were killed, including a 6-year-old boy, and 10 people were injured. Officials are still working to determine what happened and why.
 Speaking less than 10 miles away in the suburb of Park City, Trump expressed “profound sympathy.”
 “We grieve for the beautiful lives that were lost, and pray for those who were tragically injured. What a horrible event,” Trump said roughly 90 minutes into a campaign rally.
 This image provided by KAKE shows police on the scene where a person drove a vehicle through a soccer field during a game in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday. 
 Wyatt Glosson/KAKE-TV/AP 
 He added: “To all victims and their families: May God be with you. And we want to get to the bottom of what happened.”
 Trump said federal authorities will work with local officials to “give them whatever help they need.”
 “We want to find out what happened,” he said.

 “If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France — a once great nation that is being conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists who hate Christianity and they hate, frankly, the Western civilization itself,” Trump said at a rally in Kansas.
 Ginning up his Republican base, Trump spoke to a large crowd in Kansas, vowing, “We’re not going to let that happen to this country.”
 Trump also claimed that “globalist left-wing politicians” in Europe are responsible for an influx of immigration which is leading to the unrest in France.
 So far, Trump’s speech has had a few protester interruptions, which the crowd has drowned out with chants and cheers.
 “How great is it to be at a Trump rally?” Trump said after one of the early interruptions.
 The TV pooler observed at least five people being escorted from the rally.

 "Everything is so expensive": In reliably red Kansas, voters feel the economic pinch
 By Betsy Klein in Park City, Kansas
 Kansas has emerged as one of the most unexpected battlegrounds this midterm cycle as Democrats are hoping they can pull off their first Senate victory in the state since 1932.
 President Donald Trump is here today making the pitch for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who’s locked in a tighter-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor.
 Trump’s presence 15 days from the election in a state he won by 16 points in 2024 underscores how Republicans have been put on defense. GOP-aligned groups have poured millions of dollars into bolstering Marshall.
 CNN spoke with voters at his Park City rally who say they remain undecided.
 For Haley Brozek, who brought her young son to see the president, the cost of living is the biggest issue motivating her decision.
 “100% lowering the prices on things. That’s probably my biggest thing,” she said. “The gas, the groceries. I’ve got kiddos, everything is so expensive.”
 Brozek told CNN she could wait until Election Day to make up her mind but was hoping to hear from Marshall “how things are going to improve.”
 The majority of attendees planned to vote for Republicans up and down the ballot. One of those Republican candidates, Sedgwick County Commissioner Jim Howell, warned that the president’s handling of economic issues could hurt his party.
 “People are feeling the economic pinch, and right now the price of gas and price of food and the price of just living has just gone up so much recently that we’re all feeling that,” he said.
 Howell added: “I think down the down ballot is really going to be impacted. … Republicans are disillusioned or apathetic right now with the choices, and Democrats are motivated.”
 Former Kansas Gov. Bill Graves, a Republican, told CNN’s Erin Burnett that he doubts Trump’s rallies will drive GOP turnout.

 A battleground district in Michigan dominates House ad reservations
 By David Wright 
 The race in Michigan’s battleground 7th District is set to see the most ad spending over the last two weeks of the midterms – nearly $20 million – as Democratic nominee Will Lawrence , a climate activist and former member of the Democratic Socialists of America, attempts to oust GOP incumbent Rep. Tom Barrett.
 The other top contests by ad reservations for the final stretch, according to AdImpact data, show heavy spending in districts where Republicans are on the defensive or that the GOP targeted in redistricting. 
The open race for Republican John James’ seat in Michigan’s 10th District, left open as he runs for governor, also reaches the top three, at about $16 million.
 Meanwhile, after unprecedented mid-decade partisan redistricting by Republicans in North Carolina, Florida, and Texas, the GOP is set to spend heavily trying to cement their hoped-for gains, with races in Florida’s 25th District, North Carolina’s 1st District, and Texas’ 34th District all among the top 10 in ad spending for the final two weeks.
 Combined, these 10 races are set to see more than $125 million in ad spending for the last two weeks of the 2026 elections.

 Abdul El-Sayed releases new video highlighting faith amid Republican attacks
 By Elise Hammond 
 Democrat US Senate candidate for Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, speaks on stage with US Representative Ayanna Pressley (L), Democrat of Massachusetts, during a midterm campaign rally in Flint, Michigan on October 18. 
 Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images 
 Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is putting his faith front and center in a new video , as he asks voters to elect him as the country’s first Muslim senator.
 El-Sayed’s faith has been the subject of attacks during the competitive campaign, with Republicans trying to cast the Democratic nominee as sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terror. President Donald Trump on Friday referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” and falsely declared that the Democratic former public health official is a “jihadist.”

 Trump is playing defense but says "that's fine"
 Analysis by Stephen Collinson 
 Spot what all these states have in common: Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa and Florida.
 Each is a state that Trump won in 2024 — and each will welcome him on midterm campaign trips over the next five days to bolster vulnerable Republican candidates.
 To be frank, this Trump country triage is a little embarrassing for the president — even though he clearly loves rallies where he gets to hang out with his most loyal MAGA supporters.
 As he headed to Kansas to try to shore up suddenly wobbling Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who no one expected to have a competitive reelection race, Trump insisted that everywhere he goes, Republicans shoot up in the polls.
 “It’s a close race. It shouldn’t be,” Trump told reporters. “I want to make sure Roger Marshall gets in … so that’s why I’m going. I think that’s fine.”
 It’s too early to say whether the president will be able to haul vulnerable Republicans over the line and save his party’s Senate majority.
 But he’s been unwilling to contemplate the idea that his own great unpopularity and dissatisfaction over his handling of the economy or the war in Iran has anything to do with GOP struggles this year.
 There’s some logic to sending a president to fire up the base — if his most committed voters don’t show up on November 3, all Republicans will be in trouble.
 But roaming deep red states with two weeks to go in an election is also a pretty defensive strategy for a president who often boasts about how he won all the critical swing states just two years ago.
